column1: # Shared aontu unit tests: the number tower. Columns (tab-separated): name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# mode: canon = unify(src).canon == expect ; gen = generate(src) deep-equals JSON(expect) ; err = generate(src) errors, message contains expect
# mode: gens = generate(src) serialised as COMPACT JSON == expect, BYTE FOR BYTE
# See docs/design/number-tower.md for the design these rows pin. The
# tower makes `number` a pure supertype over four disjoint leaves:
# PHASE 1 -- the kind lattice. `float` names the binary64 leaf; `number`
# no longer names it, it names the family.
# `number` admits every numeric leaf, and meeting it with a leaf yields
# that leaf. Two distinct leaves have no common lower bound.
# The super() ladder gains a real rung: a concrete value lifts to its
# leaf, a leaf lifts to number, and number lifts to top.
# PHASE 2 -- the exact leaves. `0d` opts a literal into an exact leaf:
# digits only is biginteger, a `.` or an exponent makes it bigdecimal.
# (These sources were ordinary bare text before this phase; the Phase 0
# baseline rows that pinned that are gone, replaced by the rows below --
# the deliberate, visible flip the baseline existed to expose.)
# One value, one rendering (D4): scale is presentation, not identity, so
# a trailing zero and an exponent form normalise away at parse. An
# INTEGRAL BIGDECIMAL still renders one decimal place, because the `0d`
# prefix names the family and not the leaf -- without the marker,
# canon(0d1e3) would reparse as a biginteger.
# R2 extends to the exact leaves: negative zero never survives.
# The two new kind keywords, and the supertype above them.
# The super() ladder reaches the new leaves.
# D2: the leaves are DISJOINT. A value of one leaf never unifies with a
# numerically equal value of another -- a cross-leaf result would have
# to pick a kind, which is the ambiguity that makes `1 & 1.0` an error.
# D6: the exactness budget is enforced at PARSE, so a one-digit
# coefficient with an enormous exponent is refused before anything tries
# to render it in plain form.
# PHASE 3 -- identity is kind AND value. For the exact leaves that means
# comparing the NUMBER, never the pointer holding it: the large-value
# rows below are what catch a Go implementation that compares *big.Int
# The other two reserved words are kind keywords now, not bare text.
# `gen` compares through a JSON decode, so both sides land in float64 and
# two distinct exact integers above 2^53 compare EQUAL. `gens` compares
# the serialised TEXT, which is what Phase 2's exact leaves need. These
# rows use only ordinary values: their job is to prove the two runners
# emit the same bytes -- compact, no spaces, keys in generated order --
# before anything exotic depends on that.
# An integral float serialises as `1`: gens pins the BYTES, canon pins
# the kind (`a:1.0` canons as {"a":1.0}). Neither mode replaces the other.
# Go's encoder escapes <, > and & by default and JS's does not, so this
# row pins the choice that makes the two runners agree.
# Compact and alphabetical in both ports, whatever the source order.
# Number rendering has to agree byte for byte at the edges of the
# fixed-notation window, exponent sign and all.
# R2: negative zero never reaches generated output.
# The digits `gen` cannot see: this and 9007199254740993 decode to the
# same float64, so only gens can tell them apart (Phase 2 relies on it).
# PHASE 1 -- lattice behaviour the contract rows above left unpinned.
# Kind meets in the other order, and against the non-numeric neighbours.
# `number` is a pure supertype, so meeting it with BOTH leaves is still
# a meet of two disjoint leaves.
# A bare kind cannot generate -- `float` behaves exactly as `number` does.
# `number` admits every route to an integer value, not just decimal ones.
# The R1 window decides the leaf, and the leaf decides the meet.
# super() beyond the numeric family, and two rungs at once.
# `float` and `number` inside disjuncts and as type constraints.
# `float` is a VALUE keyword only: as a map key, and quoted, it is text.
# Preference (*) against the split leaves. A preference is a DEFAULT, so
# a concrete peer OF THE SAME KIND overrides it -- and the numeric leaves
# are kinds, so mixing them around a preference is a conflict.
# CHANGED 2026-08-25, and these rows moved with it. The gate used to
# widen to the FAMILY, so a float default took an integer override and
# an integer default took a float one. Those are one rule in two
# directions, and the second is what made `port: *8080 | integer` --
# the default idiom docs/skill/examples.md teaches -- accept 3.5, in
# both ports, silently widening every key written that way from integer
# to number. No kind-based gate can keep the first and refuse the
# second; refusing both is the choice, because the second reaches every
# agent that learns the idiom. See status-2026-08-21.md §6.
# What it costs is here rather than hidden: the four rows below were
# `gen` rows answering the override, and are now conflicts. A document
# that means "either" still says so -- `*8080 | number` admits 3.5, and
# THESE ARE errc ROWS, NOT err ROWS, and deliberately: message text is
# not in cross-port parity but codes are (AGENTS.md, "Error codes"), so
# an `err` row on a NEW failure pins the weaker half -- it would pass
# while the two ports named the failure differently. The docs promise
# these codes to a reader by name (docs/tutorial.md, docs/how-to.md),
# which makes them public surface. Probed in both engines before they
# were written; both answer the same code for every row here.
# The SAME-kind override is untouched, which is the point of a
# preference: plain `1 & 2` is a conflict and `*1 & 2` is 2.
# And the idiom that started it: the preferred branch no longer widens
# past the kind its sibling states.
# The idiom AS WRITTEN -- two statements, not one parenthesised meet --
# because that is the shape docs/tutorial.md and the skill card teach
# and the shape a later fragment or a merged file actually produces.
# A kind peer that the default already satisfies leaves it standing...
# ...and a kind peer from the OTHER leaf is now a conflict, where it
# used to replace the default with the constraint. It had to: a default
# the constraint can never admit is an authoring mistake, and answering
# `integer` silently discarded the `1.5` the author wrote.
# A preference whose peg is itself a kind constrains nothing.
# Outside the family it is a conflict, not an override.
# PHASE 4 -- arithmetic. The exact ladder is integer < biginteger <
# bigdecimal: a mixed EXACT operation promotes to the widest operand and
# is computed exactly. `float` is off that ladder, keeping its classic
# The headline the exact leaves exist for: this is 0.30000000000000004
# A Big leaf never silently becomes a binary float, in EITHER direction
# (boru's rule, mirrored): the mix is a hard error, not a promotion.
# integer + integer is computed EXACTLY and its result must satisfy the
# R1 storage contract. Binary64 addition silently rounded sums of exact
# operands, which the tower's exact-or-error creed cannot tolerate.
# String concatenation renders the digits, never the `0d` marker --
# matching the existing rule that concatenation is about digits and not
# upper()/lower() are exact ceiling/floor on the new leaves and keep the
# PHASE 2 and PHASE 3 -- the behaviour the contract rows above left
# unpinned. Every row below was derived by the parity probe: the source
# was run through BOTH engines, with and without --canon, and only a
# result they agreed on was written down.
# CANON IS THE SURFACE THIS PHASE IS PINNED ON. `gen` of an exact VALUE
# is Phase 5's contract and the two ports do not agree on it yet: Go's
# marshaller already emits exact digits, while TypeScript's
# JSON.stringify THROWS on the bigint peg ("Do not know how to serialize
# a BigInt"), so no shared row can exist for it until Phase 5 lands the
# exact emitter. A `gen` row appears below only where the generated
# output holds no exact value at all: a `0d` run that lexed as TEXT, a
# `0d` literal used as a KEY, or a value removed by type()/hide().
# D4 -- ONE VALUE, ONE RENDERING. Scale is presentation and not identity,
# so every spelling of a value normalises to a single canon at parse.
# These are the rows that would catch the two independently written
# decimal implementations drifting apart on normalisation.
# An exponent that exactly cancels the fraction still leaves a BIGDECIMAL
# (leaf by source, D3), so the one-decimal-place marker survives.
# Separators are legal in every digit run of the literal, exponent included.
# D3 puts the sign BEFORE the marker and neither port's literal pattern
# contains one, so `-0d5` and `+0d5` are the ordinary unary operators
# applied to a `0d` literal -- which is why a leading `+` is accepted and
# erased, exactly as it is for `+5`.
# Magnitude: the exact leaves stay exact at widths no float64 could hold.
# 60 fraction digits, and the source's trailing zero is still stripped --
# normalisation does not give up at width.
# D6 -- THE EXACTNESS BUDGET, at both boundaries. The bound is 4096 for
# BOTH the coefficient digit count and the absolute scale, and it is
# checked on the SOURCE form BEFORE normalisation -- normalising
# `0d1e1000000000` is itself the resource event the bound exists to
# The row below sits on both bounds at once and is INSIDE both: its
# coefficient is exactly 4096 digits (1 + 4095) and its scale is exactly
# 4096 (4095 fraction digits minus an exponent of -1). It is accepted,
# and since the value is 10^4095/10^4096 it then normalises all the way
# down to 0d0.1 -- which is what keeps the expectation readable while the
# One digit more of coefficient (4097), with the scale still inside
# (4095), isolates the COEFFICIENT half of the bound.
# One more of scale (4097), with the coefficient still at 4096, isolates
# the SCALE half -- the two bounds are checked independently.
# The scale bound refuses in BOTH directions, and a short literal reaches
# it from either side: `e-4097` is scale +4097, `e4097` is scale -4097.
# An exponent far beyond any machine integer is refused by the same bound
# rather than overflowing a scale field or hanging.
# The budget bounds a BIGDECIMAL (D6). A biginteger has no scale to blow
# up, so it stays exact past the coefficient bound: 4097 digits here.
# THE REJECTED AND ADJACENT FORMS -- where the lexer edges live. D3
# rejects `0d.5`, `0d-5` and a bare `0d`, and deliberately leaves what
# they do INSTEAD to fall out of the ordinary grammar. Several of the
# results below are ugly; they are pinned anyway, because an ugly agreed
# behaviour is worth more pinned than unpinned, and these are the rows
# that would notice either port's matcher changing what it claims.
# A run that cannot be a literal is bare TEXT, exactly as it was before
# A separator may only sit BETWEEN digits, so one opening the run is not
# part of the literal and the whole run is text.
# `0d.5`: the marker needs a digit, so `0d` is text and `.5` is member
# access -- the source becomes a path reference and fails to resolve.
# `0d-5`: the sign belongs before the prefix. The literal never sees the
# `-`, and no rule alternative accepts it there.
# A separator closing a run, or repeated inside one, ends the literal
# early and leaves a stray `_` -- the same refusal `1_` already gets.
# The dot-adjacency family (D3's open edge). A trailing `.` is claimed by
# the literal ONLY when a digit follows, so each of these lexes as an
# exact literal FOLLOWED BY member access and dies as an unresolvable
# path. `0d5.foo` is the case that used to differ between the ports (text
# in TypeScript, a parse error in Go); it now agrees.
# THE LITERAL IN EACH STRUCTURAL POSITION.
# A `0d` run in KEY position is text, dotted forms included: the literal
# is VALUE syntax only, exactly as `float` is (see float-as-map-key).
# In disjuncts, including one spanning both exact leaves. An unresolved
# disjunct cannot generate, which is ordinary behaviour (`1|2.0` fails the
# same way) and not an exact-leaf limitation.
# Under type() and hide(): the mark keeps the value in canon and removes
# it from generated output, whichever leaf it is.
# Behind a reference, with and without a kind constraint on the far side.
# Nested, spread over, closed, and beside a comment.
# PHASE 3 -- IDENTITY IS KIND AND VALUE, at widths and shapes the
# The landed bigint-large-* rows catch a Go port comparing *big.Int
# ADDRESSES. These catch the same bug one level in: a bigdecimal's
# coefficient is a *big.Int too, so a Decimal compared field-wise with
# `==` fails here while every short decimal row still passes.
# Identity is the NUMBER, so spellings that normalise together unify, and
# spellings that do not stay apart. `0d1e3 & 0d1000` is the D4 marker
# earning its keep: the same number, a different leaf, and so an error.
# R2/D5 through unification: a negative zero is the same lattice point as
# a positive one, in both exact leaves.
# Disjunct dedup is value comparison too, so alternatives differing only
# PHASE 4 -- ARITHMETIC, the behaviour the contract rows above left
# unpinned. Derived the same way: run through BOTH engines and written
# down only where they agreed byte for byte. The whole ordered
# operand-pair table lives in its own file (number-cross-product.tsv);
# what follows is the edges -- exactness, the integer storage contract,
# no-demotion, chaining, and upper()/lower() on every numeric leaf.
# EXACT ADDITION IS ALIGN-AND-ADD, WITH NO ROUNDING ANYWHERE. Aontu has
# no rounding mode and no precision context (D6), so the only question a
# sum can raise is whether the exact answer fits the budget.
# Scale is not part of identity, so a sum RENORMALISES: two hundredths
# make a tenth, and the answer is `0d0.1` rather than `0d0.10`.
# A sum whose exact answer needs MORE coefficient digits than either
# operand had -- the case a fixed-width representation would have to
# round, and this one simply widens.
# Unequal scales align on the wider one; the narrower operand is padded.
# A wide scale SPAN is where alignment inflates a coefficient: this one
# needs 21 coefficient digits to hold two one-digit operands, and stays
# exact rather than meeting in the middle.
# The headline case, chained: exact tenths keep adding exactly, where
# binary64 gives 0.6000000000000001 for the same three terms.
# THE BUDGET BOUNDS RESULTS, NOT ONLY LITERALS (D6). Both operands here
# are comfortably inside both bounds, and their exact sum is not: scale
# alignment needs 8001 coefficient digits. An engine with a rounding
# context would quietly return an approximation; this one refuses.
# THE INTEGER STORAGE CONTRACT, at and around its two boundaries. An
# `integer` sum is computed exactly and then has to be STORABLE: integral,
# inside the int64 window, and exactly representable in binary64. The
# third clause is the parity-critical one -- Go's int64 holds sums this
# port's double cannot -- and it is why the rows either side of 2^53 come
# in pairs, one accepted and one refused, rather than as a single limit.
# Below and at 2^53 every integer is representable, so these are values.
# Above 2^53 only the EVEN integers are representable, so a sum lands or
# is refused according to the value and not the magnitude: +2 is a value,
# +1 is an error -- and the error names the escape rather than rounding.
# THE ESCAPE THE HINT NAMES, executed: the same sum with the addend
# written `0d1` is exact, and its result is a biginteger.
# The negative mirror of the same boundary, refusal and all.
# A sum of two powers of two above 2^53 is still exact -- 2^53+2^53 is
# 2^54 -- so the rule really is exactness and not magnitude.
# THE OTHER BOUNDARY: the int64 window. 2^62+2^62 is 2^63, one past
# int64's maximum, and is refused even though a binary64 holds it
# exactly -- all three clauses of the contract must hold, not any one.
# (Its negative mirror lands exactly ON int64's minimum and is accepted
# by both ports, but they render that value differently: it is an
# integer-kind value above 2^53 needing more than 17 significant digits,
# which is entry 1 of the parity ledger. See divergent.tsv -- and note
# that operands like 2^62 are EXACT, so Phase 6's lossy-literal refusal
# RESULTS NEVER DEMOTE. The result kind follows the OPERAND kinds, not
# the value: a biginteger sum that would fit an int64 is still a
# biginteger, and a bigdecimal sum that is integral is still a
# bigdecimal. Demotion would make a document change leaf under a value
# edit, which is the whole reason the ladder is written on kinds.
# No-demotion, enforced through UNIFICATION rather than read off canon:
# an integral bigdecimal result unifies with a bigdecimal and NOT with
# the numerically equal biginteger, because the leaves are disjoint (D2).
# CHAINED AND PARENTHESISED. `+` is left-associative, so a chain climbs
# the ladder one step at a time and the widest operand anywhere in it
# decides the leaf -- including when the widening operand comes last.
# A float anywhere in the chain still refuses to meet an exact leaf, in
# either order -- the parentheses only decide WHERE the refusal happens.
# SPACING AROUND THE OPERATOR. A `0d` literal must not claim a leading
# sign, or `0d1 +0d2` would lex as a two-element implicit LIST while the
# identical `1 +2` stayed an addition. Both spellings are additions, in
# a map value and inside a list.
# The same sums in every structural position.
# PREF AND DISJUNCT OPERANDS. A pref operand contributes its PREFERRED
# VALUE, and therefore that value's kind too, so the ladder sees through
# the mark in both spellings and on either side.
# A DISJUNCT operand is not a value yet, so there is nothing to add: the
# op stays unresolved and carries the whole disjunct in its canon. This
# is ordinary `+` behaviour and not an exact-leaf limitation.
# upper() AND lower() ON EVERY NUMERIC LEAF. They are exact ceiling and
# floor, and they KEEP the argument's kind (R5) -- so a bigdecimal
# ceiling is a bigdecimal, with the one decimal place the leaf always
# renders, and a biginteger is already integral and comes back unchanged.
# The exact halves are the rows that would catch a float64 sneaking in:
# there is no round-half-even here, only ceiling and floor.
# Rounding toward zero folds a sign away, and R2/D5 says the answer is
# A biginteger is integral already: ceiling and floor are identities on
# it, and neither may demote it to an `integer`.
# The float and integer leaves are unchanged by the tower: R5 kind
# contagion already said upper()/lower() keep their operand's kind, and
# a float ceiling still renders as a float.
# Exact ceiling at the extreme of the scale budget, and of a computed
# value: neither goes anywhere near a binary64.
# PHASE 5 -- generate. The exact leaves reach JSON as exact digits: a
# JSON number is arbitrary-precision text, so the format was never the
# obstacle -- only JavaScript's serialiser, which throws on a bigint.
# These are `gens` rows (byte-exact) because that is the whole point:
# `gen` decodes through float64 and would compare two different exact
# THE GENERATE PARITY PROBE. Phase 5 is the newest surface and the one
# where the two ports have the most room to disagree: Go marshals a
# *big.Int and a *Decimal through encoding/json, TypeScript walks the
# value with its own emitter (exactJSON) because JSON.stringify throws
# on a bigint. Nothing structural is shared, so the rows below sweep the
# surface rather than sample it -- every leaf at several magnitudes and
# both signs, both zeros, an integral bigdecimal beside the biginteger
# of the same value, a long fraction, every structural position, and a
# document carrying all seven kinds at once. Each was run through BOTH
# CLIs and both compact emitters and agreed byte for byte.
# The CLI's INDENTED output was probed the same way and also agrees.
# That is not directly assertable here -- the suite has no indented mode
# -- and it is worth stating because it is where the drift actually was:
# Go's CLI used json.MarshalIndent, whose default HTML escaping rewrote
# every <, > and & in a string value as a \u00xx escape while TypeScript
# left them alone. The gens mode had already turned that escaping off
# on its own side, so no row could see it. Fixed in go/cmd/aontu (with
# a byte-exact test there, since no spec row reaches the CLI); the
# html-chars row below pins the same choice where both runners read it.
# Zero of each exact leaf, including D5's negative zeros, which must
# reach JSON as plain 0 / 0.0 and never as -0.
# Magnitudes: a biginteger far past any float64, and its negation.
# A long fraction on both sides of the point -- 30 digits either way,
# which no binary64 and no fixed 34-digit decimal context would keep.
# THE PAIR THAT MAKES THE POINT: an integral bigdecimal and a biginteger
# of the same numeric value are different lattice points, and their JSON
# differs too -- 1000.0 against 1000. (Bytes are still not the whole
# contract: see the per-port API tests, which pin the runtime object.)
# Structural positions: an exact leaf as the WHOLE document, as a list
# root, and inside a list of maps.
# Keys sort in both ports, exact values included.
# EVERY KIND IN ONE DOCUMENT: string, boolean, null, integer, float,
# biginteger, bigdecimal. Note `b:2.0` is a float and serialises as `2`
# while `d:0d4.5` keeps its exact digits -- gens sees bytes, not kinds.

column3: a:1 b:2.0 c:0d3 d:0d4.5 e:str f:true g:null

column1: # HTML characters stay literal beside an exact value: neither port may
# escape them (this is the CLI divergence described above).
# Computed exact values reach JSON by the same path as literal ones.
# PHASE 6 -- a lossy integer literal is refused, not rounded. The rule
# is EXACTNESS, not magnitude: a huge literal that lands exactly on a
# binary64 value is still a value. (0x10...0 is 2^124, a power of two,
# so it is exact -- which is why it is NOT among the flipped rows,
# contrary to what the design and G1 both said before this phase
# The refusal has an exact escape: write it as a 0d literal.
# EXACT INTEGER RENDERING -- canon prints the true digits of an
# integer-kind value, not JavaScript's shortest round-tripping form.
# These were the parity ledger's last entry (issue #21). TypeScript's
# Number.toString emits at most 17 significant digits, so 2^60 rendered
# as 1152921504606847000 -- a DIFFERENT integer that merely rounds to
# the same double -- while Go printed the true value from its int64.
# Both routes into the window are pinned: the literal, and the exact
# sum D6 opened (whose operands are individually exact, so Phase 6
# The same exactness in GENERATED JSON. Canon and the bytes are separate
# contracts, and closing issue #21 needs both: JSON.stringify of the JS
# number reproduces the very 17-digit form canon just stopped emitting,
# so the emitter has to be part of the fix.
# The three control rows below the divergent ones matter as much: the
# safe-integer maximum, its successor 2^53, and an ordinary small value
# must keep the bytes they always had, so exactness above the window
# cannot be bought by changing the rendering of everything beneath it.
# THE THIRD RENDERING SITE: `+`'s string coercion.
# Canon and the generated bytes were fixed when #21 was closed. This is the
# same one-character mistake -- String(peg) on a JS number -- at a site
# nobody had enumerated, so `"" + 2^60` produced 1152921504606847000, a
# DIFFERENT integer, where Go produced the exact digits.
# Both routes into the window are pinned, and both operand orders. The
# float rows below are the control: a float's shortest form IS the right
# answer and is what Go prints too, so `q+1.0` must stay "q1" and `q+1e21`
# must stay "q1e+21". A fix that rendered every number exactly would pass
# the integer rows and break these.
